source.title: Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs

record.tranche_reason: The study develops and tests scaling of cross-modal alignment, not held-out cross-entropy loss or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its alignment findings do not test any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper reports alignment metrics such as Flickr retrieval R@1 and WIT mutual 10-NN, rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy. Its proposed empirical law is for alignment, so those findings are recorded under fits_no_version, not linked to V1–V7.
record.test_reason: The study fits an empirical law for cross-modal alignment: Flickr R@1 of BERT-S text JEPAs against frozen DINOv2, as a function of good-view fraction q, samples seen M and unique images N. It measures no held-out pretraining loss, fits no power law in parameters, tokens or compute, and examines no compute-optimal split. Scaling laws appear only as a one-sentence motivation for Section 4.4. Retrieval R@1 is a cross-modal alignment construct rather than a language model's downstream task score, so it does not bear on V6 either. The alignment law is therefore recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors present the alignment law as an empirical summary of one recipe, not a consequence of their theory. It predicts unseen runs within seed noise up to about twice its fitted range and overestimates very long good-view runs, having no term for repeated data. They make no claim about language-model loss laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits an empirical law for cross-modal alignment from JEPA training conditions; it does not measure the held-out cross-entropy loss or fit the parameter/token allocation laws in the cited scaling-law studies.
record.method_sensitivity: The alignment fit depends on the fraction of good views, sample count and unique images. At 320M samples it overestimates results for q=1 and q=.1, and the text notes that repeated data are not represented in the law. The authors also state that the exponents are poorly identified and change when the fit range changes.

fits_no_version.finding: For one BERT-S JEPA recipe on the texts of 10.2M images, Flickr R@1 follows R@1 = a + d log M + b log(1 + q^α M^β N^γ / c). The 45-cell fit has RMSE .007. Prediction RMSE on 85 unseen random runs is .0093, versus a .0096 seed-to-seed difference. At 320M samples the law overestimates the runs with good views (q=1: .418 vs .455; q=.1: .348 vs .389) but matches q=0 (.338 vs .337).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under one JEPA recipe, cross-modal alignment follows an empirically fitted law in samples seen and good-view fraction that predicts unseen runs within seed noise, but overestimates heavily repeated-data training with good views.

fits_no_version.finding: On the same corpus, a 109M good-view JEPA reaches WIT alignment .109 after 21.6M samples; next-token prediction reaches .111 after 900M samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The choice of positive views changes the sample efficiency of cross-modal alignment by more than an order of magnitude relative to next-token prediction.

record.problems: The alignment scaling law is an empirical summary of one recipe, not a theorem; the authors state its exponents are poorly identified and depend on the fitting range. It overestimates some long repeated-data runs. The study does not measure the claimed held-out cross-entropy losses or compute-optimal allocation.
record.rows_left_out: Other alignment comparisons and downstream captioning/classification results were not extracted because they do not add evidence about the alignment scaling-law fit beyond the selected rows; see Sections 3–5 and Tables 1–18.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute is reported.
No loss extrapolation. Only the alignment law's extrapolation is tested (r2–r5).
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is studied.
Width and depth are varied only for alignment (BERT-T/S/B/L), not for loss at fixed parameters.
No power law in loss is fitted for any other modality or regime. The alignment law is log-linear in M with a power-law good-view term.
No downstream task performance of language models is related to scale or loss. LM alignment versus size (Table 16) measures PRH alignment, not a task.
Fit-dependence of loss-law exponents is not studied. The authors note only that their own alignment-law exponents are poorly identified.

record.verdict_notes: Relation could equally be cites_only. The only link to the claim is the sentence "Scaling laws turned the training of language models from trial and error into prediction," with no citation of the originals. Unrecorded but irrelevant to V1–V7: the first-registered (v1) alignment law, fitted on 33 cells (RMSE .0067), predicted the 40M/80M cells with RMSE .0115. The v1 iso-alignment exponent was M^-0.57, against M^-0.30 for the 45-cell refit, showing poorly identified exponents. A simpler law in good-view samples qM alone underestimated the 80M cells by .019–.055. This fit-dependence concerns the alignment law, not loss laws, so it is not linked to V7.
